plain.title: Set-universe closure: naturals, subsets, powersets, indexed unions

blocks.text: A set-universe is itself a set whose members are sets, and it is required to remain closed under four specified operations. It contains the natural numbers; it contains every subset of any member; it contains the power set of any member (the set of all its subsets); and it contains the union of a family of member sets whenever the indexing set is also a member.

Subset closure and power-set closure are distinct. Knowing that each subset B of A lies in the universe does not, by that clause alone, say that the collection of all those subsets belongs to it as one set. These size conventions let the notes discuss collections of mathematical structures while keeping explicit which sets are admitted.

plain.title: Russell argument: a universe is not its own member

blocks.text: Russell's argument shows that a set-universe U satisfying the stated subset-closure rule cannot itself be one of its own members. Assume U ∈ U. Then the selection R of all A ∈ U for which A ∉ A is a subset of U, so subset closure would put R in U. Asking whether R belongs to itself now forces opposite answers.

The point is not that mathematicians may never discuss a universe as a mathematical object. Rather, U cannot be a member of itself under these assumptions. The later convention places a smaller universe inside a larger one, where the smaller universe can be handled as a set without the self-membership contradiction.

plain.title: Objects, hom sets, identities, typed composition, unit and associativity laws

blocks.text: A strict category provides objects and, for each ordered pair of objects x,y, a hom set C(x,y) of morphisms from x to y. Every object has an identity arrow, and every composable pair f:x→y and g:y→z has a specified composite g∘f:x→z. The source and target matter: an arbitrary pair of arrows cannot necessarily be composed.

Two laws control these operations. Identities are neutral on both sides, and composition is associative: different parenthesizations of the same composable chain give the same morphism. A category is therefore more than a directed graph. It specifies composition with laws. In the notes, the object and hom collections are large sets under the chosen universe convention.

plain.title: Isomorphism, inverse and isomorphic objects

blocks.text: An isomorphism is a morphism f:x→y with a morphism g:y→x in the same category such that g∘f is the identity of x and f∘g is the identity of y. Both equations are required. The arrow g is called an inverse, and the objects x and y are then called isomorphic.

Isomorphic objects can be structurally interchangeable without being literally equal as elements of the category's object set. Invertibility is a property of a particular morphism together with the specified composition laws, not simply the existence of some return-looking arrow between the same endpoints.

One must check that the inverse is an allowed morphism of the same structural kind.

plain.title: Functor object/map data and preservation laws

blocks.text: A functor F:C→D translates one category into another. It assigns an object Fx of D to each object x of C and an arrow Ff:Fx→Fy to every arrow f:x→y. The assignment on arrows is not independent of the assignment on objects: the sources and targets must match.

Two conditions make the translation functorial. Identity arrows go to identity arrows, and the image of a composite g∘f is Fg∘Ff. A functor therefore preserves the organization of arrows, not merely the labels of objects. It need not be one-to-one on objects or morphisms unless additional properties are imposed.

plain.title: Forgetful, added basepoint, free vector space, discrete and indiscrete functors

blocks.text: The examples show several ways that a functor can forget or create mathematical structure. Forgetful functors send pointed sets, vector spaces and topological spaces to their underlying sets, and act on morphisms by forgetting the extra conditions. plain.title: Terminal strict category [0]

blocks.text: The terminal strict category [0] has exactly one object, usually denoted *, and exactly one morphism, its identity. There are no additional objects, non-identity arrows or choices of composition to specify.

plain.title: Precomposition and postcomposition functors; whiskering

blocks.text: Given F:C→D, one can use it to transform other functors in two ways. Precomposition takes a functor G:D→E and changes its input by forming G∘F:C→E. Postcomposition takes a functor G:E→C and changes its output by forming F∘G:E→D.

Both constructions act on natural transformations as well as on functors. On components, precomposition evaluates the old transformation at Fx; postcomposition applies F to the old component. The different domains and codomains must be kept straight. The notes give these constructions and leave their functoriality checks to the reader.

plain.title: Contravariant Yoneda bijection, evaluation at identity and naturality in c,F

blocks.text: The Yoneda lemma begins with a locally small category C, an object c, and a contravariant set-valued functor F:Cᵒᵖ→Set. One direction is described by evaluating a natural transformation at the identity arrow of c. The notes also provide the candidate reverse construction and assign the remaining well-definedness, inverse and naturality checks. The conceptual message is that a natural rule for interpreting every map into c is determined by information at c itself. plain.title: Yoneda functor on objects and morphisms

blocks.text: The Yoneda functor y_C assigns to each object c of a locally small category C its representable presheaf C(−,c). To a morphism f:c→d, it assigns the natural transformation obtained by postcomposing incoming arrows with f.

The construction is covariant as a functor from C into the functor category of presheaves, even though each representable presheaf is contravariant in its argument. The notes leave verification that this assignment is itself a functor as an exercise.

plain.title: Fully faithful means bijective on each hom set

blocks.text: A functor F:C→D is fully faithful when, for every fixed pair of source objects x and y, its map C(x,y)→D(Fx,Fy) is a bijection. Faithful means that different arrows between those fixed objects are not identified; full means that every arrow between their two images comes from an arrow in C.

These conditions concern morphisms between image objects. They do not assert that every object in D is the image of an object of C. That additional issue belongs to essential surjectivity, discussed later. The fixed-pair qualification is important: fully faithful does not mean the functor must use distinct names for every source object.

blocks.text: The informal (infinity,1)-category described in these notes has potentially non-invertible 1-morphisms. Composition need not obey associativity and unit laws as literal equations of all the chosen data; instead there are specified higher invertible morphisms relating the different composites.

Those higher comparisons must themselves satisfy compatibility conditions, often called coherence. It is not enough to say that every pair of ways of composing is “roughly the same.” One also has to ensure that the comparisons between those ways are mutually consistent. This is motivation for later axioms, not a claim that the full coherence structure has already been formalized in ordinary Lean categories.

plain.title: Paths and homotopies fixing endpoints/boundaries

blocks.text: A path is a continuous journey through a topological space, with a specified starting point and endpoint. When two paths fit end to end, we can concatenate them. However, the resulting parameterized path depends on how the time interval is divided: joining three paths as (first then second) then third need not give literally the same function as first then (second then third).

A homotopy gives a continuous deformation between paths while keeping their endpoints fixed. These alternative concatenations agree up to such a deformation, and following a path by its own reverse is homotopic to remaining at the starting point. This is a model for composition that behaves correctly up to higher comparison rather than strict equality.

“So our route book must remember the transformations between journeys, not just the journeys themselves,” she said. The mapmaker nodded: higher-dimensional comparisons were part of the story, not an optional decoration.

blocks.text: In the motivating example from topology, objects are points, 1-morphisms are paths, and 2-morphisms are endpoint-fixed homotopies of paths. A path followed by its reverse is equivalent, up to homotopy, to a constant path. Thus even the 1-morphisms are invertible up to the relevant higher comparison.

This is more than an ordinary groupoid: an ordinary fundamental groupoid records homotopy classes of paths but does not retain the full tower of higher homotopies. The notes use this example to show how topological spaces naturally motivate structures with invertibility in every positive dimension.

blocks.text: In homotopy type theory, the fundamental entities are types and their terms. For terms x,y:X, the expression x=y is itself an identity type. Its inhabitants represent identifications of x with y, often pictured as paths. Two such identifications can themselves be compared by another identity type, and this process can continue.

This gives a type higher-dimensional structure analogous to an infinity-groupoid. Unlike a yes-or-no interpretation of equality between elements of a set, the intended identity type can carry information about how an identification occurs. The lecture notes present this as the proposed foundation for their later synthetic theory; ordinary proof-irrelevant equality in Lean is not a substitute for this entire higher structure.

plain.title: Indiscernibility, transport and Structure Identity Principle

blocks.text: In ordinary set-based mathematics, the equation x = y allows us to substitute one expression for the other. A group isomorphism is different: it is a structure-preserving correspondence between groups that may have different underlying sets. Thus the property “contains an element of order two” survives isomorphism, while “its identity element is literally the number 0” depends on a particular presentation.

The lecture notes describe a stronger foundational idea from homotopy type theory, the Structure Identity Principle: identifications between groups correspond to group isomorphisms. Identity then records how two groups are identified, not merely whether two sets happen to be written with identical elements. Combined with transport along identifications, this ensures that properties expressible in that structural language are invariant under isomorphism. This higher foundational principle is announced here; it is not established by the ordinary-category Lean models alone.

blocks.text: Two royal clerks arrived at Mira's desk with what they insisted were different mathematical treasures. The first carried a little group whose elements were 0 and 1, combined by addition modulo two. The second carried a group with elements 1 and −1, combined by multiplication.

“Mine has zero as its identity,” the first clerk declared. “Mine has one,” said the second. “Surely they are different in every way.” Mira asked each clerk to point out an element which, combined with itself, gave the identity but was not the identity. Both clerks succeeded.

She drew a correspondence: 0 went to 1, and 1 went to −1. The operation tables matched under her translation. “Your printed symbols differ,” she told them, “but as groups the two structures are isomorphic.”

The queen then asked a more difficult question. “Could our mathematical language treat that isomorphism as the very way these groups are identified, rather than as a second-class relation between different presentations?” Mira opened a volume on homotopy type theory. In its intended setting, the Structure Identity Principle offers precisely that connection.

The clerks left with different labels still written on their scrolls, but no longer mistook the labels for the structure. Mira marked the higher foundational claim for later study rather than stamping it as proved by today's strict-category exercises.

In a strict category, the objects form a set, and equalities of objects can be taken literally. plain.title: Identities do not change a composite

plain.title: Set-universe closure: naturals, subsets, powersets, indexed unions

plain.title: Isomorphism, inverse and isomorphic objects

blocks.text: An isomorphism is a morphism f:x→y with a morphism g:y→x in the same category such that g∘f is the identity of x and f∘g is the identity of y. Both equations are required. The arrow g is called an inverse, and the objects x and y are then called isomorphic.

Isomorphic objects can be structurally interchangeable without being literally equal as elements of the category's object set. Invertibility is a property of a particular morphism together with the specified composition laws, not simply the existence of some return-looking arrow between the same endpoints.

plain.title: Bijections, pointed bijections, linear bijections and homeomorphisms

blocks.text: What counts as an isomorphism depends on the category. In Set it is a bijection; in pointed Set it is a bijection preserving the marked points; in Vect_k it is a linear bijection; and in Top it is a homeomorphism, a continuous bijection whose inverse is also continuous.

The last distinction is important. A continuous bijection between topological spaces does not always have a continuous inverse. Merely counting elements or finding a set-theoretic inverse therefore cannot establish an isomorphism in every category. One must check that the inverse is an allowed morphism of the same structural kind.

plain.title: Functor object/map data and preservation laws

blocks.text: A functor F:C→D translates one category into another. It assigns an object Fx of D to each object x of C and an arrow Ff:Fx→Fy to every arrow f:x→y. The assignment on arrows is not independent of the assignment on objects: the sources and targets must match.

Two conditions make the translation functorial. Identity arrows go to identity arrows, and the image of a composite g∘f is Fg∘Ff. A functor therefore preserves the organization of arrows, not merely the labels of objects. It need not be one-to-one on objects or morphisms unless additional properties are imposed.

plain.title: Forgetful, added basepoint, free vector space, discrete and indiscrete functors

blocks.text: The examples show several ways that a functor can forget or create mathematical structure. Forgetful functors send pointed sets, vector spaces and topological spaces to their underlying sets, and act on morphisms by forgetting the extra conditions. Other functors start with a set: one adjoins a new distinguished point, another forms the free vector space with the set as a basis, and two equip the set with the discrete or indiscrete topology.

These constructions must work on functions as well as on objects. Discrete topology makes every subset open; indiscrete topology makes only the empty and whole sets open. A free vector space consists of finite linear combinations of basis elements, not merely a set with a decorative “vector” label.

plain.title: Contravariant functors as functors from the opposite

blocks.text: A contravariant functor from C to D is, by definition, an ordinary functor Cᵒᵖ→D. On objects it still assigns Fx to each x, but an arrow f:x→y becomes an arrow Ff:Fy→Fx: the direction is reversed.

This is not arbitrary shorthand; it follows from applying a standard functor to the opposite category. Contravariance is useful whenever changing a source object naturally pulls data back rather than pushing it forward.

plain.title: Component types and naturality square

plain.title: Fully faithful means bijective on each hom set

blocks.text: A functor F:C→D is fully faithful when, for every fixed pair of source objects x and y, its map C(x,y)→D(Fx,Fy) is a bijection. plain.title: Left/right adjoints, unit, counit and both triangle identities

blocks.text: An adjunction L⊣R relates two functors L:C→D and R:D→C by a unit η:id_C⇒R L and a counit ε:L R⇒id_D. The unit compares an object x with the result of going from C to D and back; the counit compares going from D to C and back with an object y of D.

These comparisons must satisfy two triangle identities. Roughly, if one makes the appropriate round trip and then applies the appropriate comparison, the result is the identity transformation on the relevant adjoint. Adjunction is not the same as equivalence: unit and counit of a general adjunction need not be isomorphisms. The exact domains and component equations matter more than the loose phrase “the functors undo one another.”

plain.title: Essential surjectivity up to object isomorphism

blocks.text: A functor F:C→D is essentially surjective if every target object d in D is isomorphic to at least one object of the form Fc for some c in C. It does not require d to equal Fc literally, and it does not require the object function of F to be onto.

For each d, one needs an actual source object c and an actual isomorphism Fc≅d. Essential surjectivity is one ingredient of the later equivalence criterion; alone it does not establish full faithfulness.

plain.title: Paths and homotopies fixing endpoints/boundaries

blocks.text: A path is a continuous journey through a topological space, with a specified starting point and endpoint. When two paths fit end to end, we can concatenate them. However, the resulting parameterized path depends on how the time interval is divided: joining three paths as (first then second) then third need not give literally the same function as first then (second then third).

A homotopy gives a continuous deformation between paths while keeping their endpoints fixed. These alternative concatenations agree up to such a deformation, and following a path by its own reverse is homotopic to remaining at the starting point. This is a model for composition that behaves correctly up to higher comparison rather than strict equality.

plain.title: Indiscernibility, transport and Structure Identity Principle

blocks.text: In ordinary set-based mathematics, the equation x = y allows us to substitute one expression for the other. A group isomorphism is different: it is a structure-preserving correspondence between groups that may have different underlying sets. Thus the property “contains an element of order two” survives isomorphism, while “its identity element is literally the number 0” depends on a particular presentation.

The lecture notes describe a stronger foundational idea from homotopy type theory, the Structure Identity Principle: identifications between groups correspond to group isomorphisms. Identity then records how two groups are identified, not merely whether two sets happen to be written with identical elements. Combined with transport along identifications, this ensures that properties expressible in that structural language are invariant under isomorphism. This higher foundational principle is announced here; it is not established by the ordinary-category Lean models alone.

plain.title: Equality, isomorphism and equivalence-sensitive invariance

blocks.text: A strict isomorphism of categories requires strictly inverse functors, which in particular forces an exact bijection between their object sets. Categorical equivalence relaxes that requirement: it allows objects to be recovered up to isomorphism. Consequently, a category with one object can be equivalent to a category with two different but isomorphic objects.

This matters for the course's larger motivation. Constructions that depend on literal object names or equality of presentations need not respect categorical equivalence. The synthetic approach announced later aims to treat sameness in a way that builds structural invariance into the foundations. These pages motivate that goal but do not yet prove the later synthetic axioms.

blocks.text: An inspector came to the palace with two ledgers. One listed a single room; the other listed north and south separately, joined by unique reversible permits. “The ledgers have different numbers of entries,” he proclaimed. “They cannot describe the same kind of structure.”

Mira did not deny the arithmetic. The first ledger had one object name; the second had two. But when she examined the permitted routes, the two rooms of the second ledger were isomorphic. A translation could preserve the structural relationships without giving an exact inverse bijection between printed names.

Fern suggested that the kingdom should stop treating every naming difference as a mathematical difference. Mira agreed — cautiously. Sometimes literal presentations mattered for a particular purpose, but statements intended to describe categorical structure ought to respect the appropriate notion of equivalence.
On the next page of her notebook she wrote “synthetic foundations” and left room for the later theory that would develop this principle more systematically.

plain.title: Contravariant Yoneda bijection, evaluation at identity and naturality in c,F

blocks.text: The Yoneda lemma begins with a locally small category C, an object c, and a contravariant set-valued functor F:Cᵒᵖ→Set. It relates two apparently different kinds of information: natural transformations from the representable C(−,c) to F, and elements of the set F(c). The relation is a bijection, natural in both c and F.

One direction is described by evaluating a natural transformation at the identity arrow of c. The notes also provide the candidate reverse construction and assign the remaining well-definedness, inverse and naturality checks. The conceptual message is that a natural rule for interpreting every map into c is determined by information at c itself. This is a precise categorical correspondence, not merely a claim that c has a recognizable personality.

blocks.text: Mira guarded a tower c where travelers arrived from many cities. A mysterious registry F assigned information to every city, changing contravariantly when routes were followed backwards.

The queen proposed a demanding system of labels. For every city x and every permitted journey from x to c, Mira would assign a label belonging to F(x). And her labels had to remain compatible when someone approached x by another route. A careless collection of independent labels would not pass the test.

Fern asked whether Mira really had to invent labels for infinitely many incoming journeys separately. The queen pointed to the identity journey at c, the tower's own stay-here permit. The Yoneda lemma claimed that one suitable piece of information there would correspond to an entire natural labeling system for incoming journeys.

Mira placed the correspondence on the blackboard. The source notes displayed the candidate formulas, but the students still had to check their naturality and inverse properties. The story offered a reason to care about the result: a global pattern of compatible observations is controlled by one local piece of data.
